Telling a real SINE family from everything else

Given a set of genomic loci proposed as one family — the output of a sear search from a consensus — decide whether it is a real SINE family, refine its boundaries, and say which copies are contaminants. This page is the working record: what each variable measures, which survived testing, twenty-four worked examples with their verdicts, and the one case it still gets wrong.

THE PROBLEM

What is actually being decided

A search returns a few thousand loci that matched a consensus. Some proposed families are real. Others are junk, or a real family with junk mixed in, or two families that should be separated, or copies sitting inside some other repeat. The manual method is to align ~100 copies with their flanks and judge the shape of the alignment in about a second. This formalises that judgement.

It has three tiers, and the answer is not binary:

  • Tier 1 — alignability. Do the copies align to each other at all?
  • Tier 2 — boundary structure. Is there a robustly aligned core, with similarity collapsing sharply to genomic background on both sides?
  • Tier 3 — internal homogeneity. Is it one element throughout, or do different copies carry different blocks?
The output is a score plus named sub-cases, not accept/reject. "Not a SINE" is several different things — no element at all, an element with contaminants, two subfamilies needing separation, copies nested in another repeat — and each implies different follow-up work. A set that scores badly but contains 20–30 genuine copies is still worth reporting: that is where the next clean family comes from.
METHOD

How a set is measured

  1. Extract each copy with 70 bp of real genomic flank. Not 300 bp — that forces the aligner to align unrelated DNA and smears a 250 bp element across 1200 columns.
  2. Align with the known subfamily consensus added as a row. Its first and last nucleotide delimit the element: no threshold, no free parameter, and nothing that moves when the copies are resampled.
  3. De-gap the flanks and push them against the element. There is nothing homologous out there to align, so aligning it only manufactures similarity.
  4. Measure per copy, never on a collapsed average, and measure flank identity on ungapped sequence walking outward from each copy's own edge.
  5. Refine and prune: search the boundary around the consensus edge, drop copies that do not support the consensus, re-score.
VARIABLESWhat each one means

The variables, and which survived testing

Every variable was swept against 14 synthetic gradients of 100 sets each, one parameter varied at a time. Responds to below counts how many of those 14 gradients the variable moves with. One or two means a diagnostic; many means a general quality score — useful for ranking candidates, useless for saying what is wrong.

Sorted by specificity. ρ is Spearman correlation against the swept parameter.
Confounds found, and what was done about them. Correlation alone was misleading here: Spearman rho flags any monotone trend regardless of size, so several apparent confounds turned out to be drifts of 0.005. Effect size settles it.
  • Fixed — the support threshold now scales with the family's own contrast instead of a constant 0.55, so an old but clean family is no longer called contaminated. Age now costs 0.12 of frac_supported against 0.49 for real contamination.
  • Fixed — sub_gap is measured against a random-split null. The copy-number confound went from ρ −0.97 to −0.11; the residual age drift is 0.005 against a real signal of 0.078.
  • Fixed — seg_diag ran on aligned columns, where the aligner puts a swapped segment back where it came from. On unaligned slots a fully scrambled set now reads 0.42 against 0.84–0.92 for clean families.
  • Fixed — structure is now tested after pruning, not before: contamination was masking scrambling (ρ −0.61 → −0.92 once contamination is low).
  • Not fixed — cliff is substantially an age measure: age moves it by 0.43 of a 0.64 range. Use frac_supported as the primary Tier-2 statistic instead, which is now age-normalised by construction.
  • Not fixed — rank1_frac correlates with age at ρ = −1.00. The spec's Tier-3 statistic is an age meter. It should be dropped, not repaired.
THE HARD CASESeparable

Telling a SINE from a LINE — and a mistake worth recording

Every negative up to here was random DNA or synthetic. The honest test is a real, abundant, ancient repeat that is genuinely not a SINE. The first attempt at one was wrong in an instructive way.

Querying the genome with the last 260 bp of a 15.4 kb LINE returned 55,000 fragments which scored 98–99. That looked like a serious failure — until the loci were intersected with the curated SINE annotation for the same genome: 66 % of them are known Tal SINEs. A SINE mobilised by a LINE carries that LINE's 3′ terminus; it is the same sequence. The set was two-thirds SINEs, and scoring it 99 was correct.

Querying the LINE interior instead — ORF territory, which no SINE carries — gives 526 loci, none overlapping a known SINE. Those score very differently:

SetScorefrac_supportedclifftsd_fracFlags
real SINE100.01.000.6360.83—
LINE 3′ terminus (66 % SINEs)99.01.000.4570.77FLANKS_UNMEASURED
real LINE interior53–581.000.360.00SHARED_FLANKS

A genuine LINE is separated by two independent signals, and neither is the cliff: tsd_frac = 0.00 against 0.83, because a LINE interior fragment is not an insertion boundary and so has no target-site duplication; and SHARED_FLANKS, because what flanks it is more LINE, not independent genomic DNA. cliff and frac_supported do not separate it at all — a LINE interior is a real conserved element, so of course its copies support their consensus.

What remains genuinely undecidable is a LINE 3′ terminus, and that is not a defect of the method. A SINE and its partner LINE's 3′ end are the same sequence, inserted by the same machinery, with the same TSDs and poly-A. No alignment-based method can separate them, because at that locus there is nothing to separate — the question is answered by whether the copy continues upstream into ORF sequence, which means looking beyond the aligned window. In practice: intersect the loci against an existing repeat annotation. It is one bedtools command and it should be a standard step.
SECOND FAMILYPartly generalises

Hedgehog, run through the identical pipeline

Every number in this project came from one SINE family type. Erinaceidae SINEs — eight curated subfamilies, a different genome and a different family — are the check.

The geometry carried over unchanged: the consensus-row anchor, short flanks and ungapped flank statistics all worked with no adjustment. Six of eight subfamilies score 68–98. But the biology did not transfer: hedgehog copies carry TSDs at 0.18 against 0.74 in Tal, and element length is 159–203 bp against 250–280.

Two subfamilies — e1-4 and e2-2 — score 3.5 and 25.9 with flank identity 0.68 against 0.28 for a normal family. Their copies are not in independent genomic contexts. Whether that is a satellite array, a duplication, or an artefact of how those subfamilies were curated is a question for Sergei, not for more computation.

RESULTSTwenty worked examples

Verdicts, weighted toward the hard cases

Deliberately not a page of clean positives. A few clear SINEs, a few clear non-SINEs, and the rest in the grey zone or carrying a named sub-case — because that is where the thresholds are still wrong. Each panel gives the verdict and its reason, the profile along the element, and the alignment.

Read the profile as: identity high and flat across the element, then falling to the dashed line — the identity of unrelated DNA, 0.25 — in the flanks. A real family has a sharp cliff at both edges. Coverage ramping up across the element means truncation. Below it sit the motif rows and the structural feature track. Hover anything for values; double-click a panel for the consensus as nucleotides.

Scope. Every biological number here comes from one SINE family type — Tal, tRNA-derived, in four talpid genomes — plus synthetic controls built from it. The A box at 12–22, the B box at 64–75, the T-tract insertion signature, TSD frequency and element length are properties of this family. The geometry — consensus-row anchoring, short flanks, ungapped flank statistics — should generalise; the biology should not be assumed to.
